comparator.sourceNotes: Current 180-EC Classics is reconstructed as 60+60+60. The formal first-listed specialisation Antieke wijsbegeerte is selected independently of UCR fit. The representative admitted profile uses Greek A and Latin B placement (no Greek school exam, Latin at school-exam level), not stacked placement levels. Year2 selects the Stoa philosophy workshop and current Greek language seminar. Year3 selects Greek Reading List and Latin Silius Italicus workshop, preserving both languages, followed by a philosophy-aligned thesis and genuine open30. Zero-credit thesis seminar and alternative options are excluded.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: The alternatives differ by twelve courses / 90 EC in each direction. The substitutions follow from the evidenced democracy-and-political-reception question.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Introductory literary studies, classical rhetoric, Western philosophy and world archaeology are placed in the first year, before the 200-level work on Greek archaeology, stylistics, myth and epic, empires and ancient warfare, and before the third-year courses on ancient democratic heritage, persuasive communication, adaptation, interpretive theory, art-historical research and the archival research seminar. No scheduled course carries a formal prerequisite, every course is offered in its assigned term, and the one 100-level course placed in year two, Introduction to Western Art History, is a deliberate entry point into the Renaissance reception strand rather than a displaced foundation.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Two complete related-fields programmes are defensible. The first is the closest feasible response through classical literature in translation, rhetoric, ancient philosophy, archaeology, history and reception. The second uses the programme’s evidenced account of antiquity’s influence on later societies to build a substantively different political, legal and historical curriculum; twelve courses / 90 EC differ in each direction. A third programme centred on Greek and Latin language, philology and original-text expertise is not feasible because the current UCR workbook contains no ancient-language sequence, Greek or Latin linguistics, or advanced original-text seminars. That central disciplinary gap remains explicit rather than being filled with general literature or communication courses.

notes.text: Leiden Classics combines cumulative Greek and Latin language acquisition, linguistics and advanced reading of classical texts in the original with literature, history, philosophy and material culture. UCR can approach classical antiquity through literature in translation, rhetoric, philosophy, archaeology, heritage, history, law and politics, but it does not teach Greek or Latin. The UCR programmes therefore offer related perspectives rather than a full Classics curriculum.

The Leiden programme follows a fixed Greek-and-Latin disciplinary sequence within the Ancient Philosophy specialisation, alongside 30 EC of open choice and a Classics thesis. UCR assembles related material across individually selected literature, communication, heritage, philosophy, history, law and politics courses; it has no separate language sequence, open-elective block or scheduled thesis. Optional independent research is shown only as the standardized comparison element.
